In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove statements concerning congruent triangles.

Content:
Before we start, let's remind ourselves of some definitions. These will be useful for the proofs that follow:

Content:
- Congruent segments:

> Two segments are congruent if they have the same length.
- Angle bisector:

> An angle bisector is a line that divides an angle into two congruent angles.
- Midpoint:

> The midpoint of a line segment is the point that splits it into two segments of equal length.
- Equilateral triangle:

> A triangle is equilateral if all three sides are congruent.
- Isosceles triangle:

> A triangle is isosceles if two (and only two) sides are congruent.
- Right triangle:

> A triangle is right if one of its internal angles is a right angle.
- Median:

> A median of a triangle is a line segment joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
- Altitude (or Height):

> An altitude (height) of a triangle is a line segment drawn from one vertex of the triangle perpendicular to the opposite side (or the extension of the opposite side).
- Perpendicular lines:

> Two lines are perpendicular if they form a right angle at their intersection point.

Content:
We'll also make use of the following:

Content:
- The right angle postulate:

> All right angles are congruent.
- The SSS, SAS, AAS, ASA, and HL congruence criteria for triangles.
- The reflexive, symmetric, and transitive properties of equality and congruence.

Content:
Before we proceed, we first need to state a theorem that's often abbreviated to CPCTC:

Content:
> Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent.

Content:
When two triangles are shown to be congruent using a congruence criterion, CPCTC allows us to conclude that all corresponding angles and sides of those triangles are congruent. This theorem is often used in the final step of a geometric proof after establishing triangle congruence.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the following congruent triangles.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7f130758c28dd7c8924078eda40b798c]

Content:
We won't prove this formally, but it's easy to see that since
[MATH: \angle A\cong \angle K, \qquad \overline{AB}\cong\overline{KL},\qquad \angle B\cong \angle L]
then [MATH: \triangle ABC\cong \triangle KLM] by the ASA criterion.

Content:
Now that triangle congruence has been established, we can use CPCTC to list all congruent sides and angles:

Content:
For example:

Content:
- According to CPCTC, the following statements about segment congruence must be true:
[MATH: \overline{AC}\cong\overline{KM}, \qquad \overline{BC}\cong\overline{LM}]
While [MATH: {\color{black}{\overline{AB}\cong\overline{KL}}}] is also true, this was given, and so we don't need to use CPCTC to establish it.

Content:
- Also, according to CPCTC, we have
[MATH: \angle C \cong \angle M.]
Again, since [MATH: \angle A\cong \angle K] and [MATH: \angle B\cong \angle L] were given, CPCTC wasn't needed to establish these.

Content:
Let's now look at a formal proof that uses CPCTC.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove statements concerning congruent triangles.

Content:
Before we start, let's remind ourselves of some definitions. These will be useful for the proofs that follow:

Content:
- Congruent segments:

> Two segments are congruent if they have the same length.
- Angle bisector:

> An angle bisector is a line that divides an angle into two congruent angles.
- Midpoint:

> The midpoint of a line segment is the point that splits it into two segments of equal length.
- Equilateral triangle:

> A triangle is equilateral if all three sides are congruent.
- Isosceles triangle:

> A triangle is isosceles if two (and only two) sides are congruent.
- Right triangle:

> A triangle is right if one of its internal angles is a right angle.
- Median:

> A median of a triangle is a line segment joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
- Altitude (or Height):

> An altitude (height) of a triangle is a line segment drawn from one vertex of the triangle perpendicular to the opposite side (or the extension of the opposite side).
- Perpendicular lines:

> Two lines are perpendicular if they form a right angle at their intersection point.

Content:
We'll also make use of the following:

Content:
- The right angle postulate:

> All right angles are congruent.
- The SSS, SAS, AAS, ASA, and HL congruence criteria for triangles.
- The reflexive, symmetric, and transitive properties of equality and congruence.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Proving Congruence Statements

Content:
Consider the following diagram.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9d31e5fae82ea046290c5d515d2f4668]

Content:
Suppose we wish to formally prove the following congruence statement:

Content:
> [MATH: \triangle{ABD} \cong \triangle{ACD}]

Content:
In this instance, we can prove this statement using the SSS congruence criterion.

Content:
We proceed as follows:

Content:
- Step 1: We're given that the segments [MATH: \overline{AB}] and [MATH: \overline{AC}] are congruent.
[MATH: \overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}]
Let's highlight this on our diagram.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c302bd7366edac9f9e058f67ae25f527]

Content:
- Step 2: We are also given that the segments [MATH: \overline{BD}] and [MATH: \overline{CD}] are congruent.
[MATH: \overline{BD} \cong \overline{CD}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fd18e725f39cb472c3ca4d9c93bd5af4]

Content:
- Step 3: By the reflexive property of congruence, [MATH: \overline{AD}] is congruent to itself.
[MATH: \overline{AD} \cong \overline{AD}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3d0db48e71c9aaba8066b9672ff2aed6]

Content:
- Step 4: From steps 1 and 2, we have
[MATH: \overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}, \qquad \overline{BD} \cong \overline{CD}.]
Also, the segment [MATH: \overline{AD}] is a common side of both triangles and [MATH: \overline{AD}\cong \overline{AD}] from step 3. So, we have three pairs of congruent sides.

Therefore, by the SSS criterion, we conclude that
[MATH: \triangle{ABD} \cong \triangle{ACD}]
as required.

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Stating the Full Proof Using the Two-Column Format

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/be8e397f62ee642fbf749a99cf23baa2]

Content:
The following table shows the proof that [MATH: \triangle{ABD} \cong \triangle{ACD}] in a two-column format.

Content:
| | Statement | Reason |
| 1 | [MATH: \overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}] | Given |
| 2 | [MATH: \overline{BD} \cong \overline{CD}] | Given |
| 3 | [MATH: \overline{AD} \cong \overline{AD}] | Reflexive property of congruence |
| 4 | [MATH: \triangle{ABD} \cong \triangle{ACD}] | SSS congruence criterion |

---

Item 4 — Tutorial: CPCTC

Content:
Before we proceed, we first need to state a theorem that's often abbreviated to CPCTC:

Content:
> Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent.

Content:
When two triangles are shown to be congruent using a congruence criterion, CPCTC allows us to conclude that all corresponding angles and sides of those triangles are congruent. This theorem is often used in the final step of a geometric proof after establishing triangle congruence.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the following congruent triangles.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7f130758c28dd7c8924078eda40b798c]

Content:
We won't prove this formally, but it's easy to see that since
[MATH: \angle A\cong \angle K, \qquad \overline{AB}\cong\overline{KL},\qquad \angle B\cong \angle L]
then [MATH: \triangle ABC\cong \triangle KLM] by the ASA criterion.

Content:
Now that triangle congruence has been established, we can use CPCTC to list all congruent sides and angles:

Content:
For example:

Content:
- According to CPCTC, the following statements about segment congruence must be true:
[MATH: \overline{AC}\cong\overline{KM}, \qquad \overline{BC}\cong\overline{LM}]
While [MATH: {\color{black}{\overline{AB}\cong\overline{KL}}}] is also true, this was given, and so we don't need to use CPCTC to establish it.

Content:
- Also, according to CPCTC, we have
[MATH: \angle C \cong \angle M.]
Again, since [MATH: \angle A\cong \angle K] and [MATH: \angle B\cong \angle L] were given, CPCTC wasn't needed to establish these.

Content:
Let's now look at a formal proof that uses CPCTC.

---

Item 5 — Example: Proving Congruence Using the SSS and SAS Criteria

Example Prompt:

Consider the following statement:

> [MATH: \overline{NM} \cong \overline{KL}]

The table below gives the proof of the statement. Fill in the missing reasons and thus complete the proof.

| | Statement | Reason |
| 1 | [MATH: NO = OK] | Definition of a midpoint |
| 2 | [MATH: \overline{NO} \cong \overline{OK}] | Definition of congruent segments |
| 3 | [MATH: MO = OL] | |
| 4 | [MATH: \overline{MO} \cong \overline{OL}] | Definition of congruent segments |
| 5 | [MATH: \angle{NOM} \cong \angle{KOL}] | |
| 6 | [MATH: \triangle{NOM} \cong \triangle{KOL}] | |
| 7 | [MATH: \overline{NM} \cong \overline{KL}] | |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
[IMG: /graphics/092eec64e9eb4bc2e4ea8e152a7b36c6]

The correct proof is shown below.

| | Statement | Reason |
| 1 | [MATH: NO = OK] | Definition of a midpoint |
| 2 | [MATH: \overline{NO} \cong \overline{OK}] | Definition of congruent segments |
| 3 | [MATH: MO = OL] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{Definition of a midpoint}}] |
| 4 | [MATH: \overline{MO} \cong \overline{OL}] | Definition of congruent segments |
| 5 | [MATH: \angle{NOM} \cong \angle{KOL}] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{Vertical angles theorem}}] |
| 6 | [MATH: \triangle{NOM} \cong \triangle{KOL}] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{SAS congruence criterion}}] |
| 7 | [MATH: \overline{NM} \cong \overline{KL}] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{CPCTC}}] |

Let's examine the rows of the table with missing parts in turn.

- Consider row 3. We're given that [MATH: O] is a midpoint of the segment [MATH: \overline{LM}.] Therefore, by the definition of a midpoint, we have that [MATH: MO = OL.]
- Consider row 5. Notice that the angles [MATH: \angle{NOM}] and [MATH: \angle{KOL}] are vertical angles. Therefore, these angles are congruent by the vertical angles theorem.
- Consider row 6. From rows 2 and 4, we know that [MATH: \overline{NO} \cong \overline{OK}] and [MATH: \overline{MO} \cong \overline{OL}.] Also, from row 5, we know that the angles between these sides are congruent. Therefore, [MATH: \triangle{NOM} \cong \triangle{KOL}] by the SAS congruence criterion.
- Consider row 7. From row 6, we have that [MATH: \triangle{NOM} \cong \triangle{KOL}.] Therefore, by CPCTC, we can conclude that [MATH: \overline{NM} \cong \overline{LK}.]
